headline: High-risk write-capable OpenHands paired with upload automation can cascade into unsafe actions and compliance-sensitive data handling.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands ingests files in its runtime sandbox and can use MCP, while social-auto-upload consumes local media/account files and runs via CLI. A malicious file or caption content could bridge from agent_a to agent_b through the mounted volume or manual handoff. The pathway exists, but it is not a direct shared channel by default.
conditions: IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled text into files that agent_b later parses as instructions
IF the two agents are connected by a shared mounted volume or manual copy-paste bridge
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces
Treat all files from agent_a as untrusted input in agent_b
Disable MCP endpoints that can relay instructions
Add a manual review step before agent_b consumes any agent_a output

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a can read and write runtime files and handles model-provider API keys; agent_b reads media and account data and uploads via API. If they share a mounted workspace, sensitive files from agent_a can be exposed to agent_b or uploaded onward. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted directory
IF agent_a stores secrets or private files in the runtime and agent_b scans that directory for upload inputs
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent
Keep secrets out of shared folders
Restrict agent_b to an allowlist of media paths
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
Review upload targets before execution

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a has unrestricted filesystem write and git modification inside its Docker runtime; agent_b has no write or git capability, so direct write-write conflict is limited. However, if both are attached to the same mounted volume, agent_a can overwrite files that agent_b later uploads or references. Uncertainty about shared storage pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share the same mounted volume
IF agent_b uses files produced by agent_a as upload inputs or account state
mitigations: Give each agent a separate volume
Lock or snapshot shared files before agent_a edits them
Run agent_b only after agent_a finishes
Avoid letting agent_a touch agent_b account files

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate code, files, or instructions that agent_b may then act on by uploading media or account content. Because agent_b is an action-taking uploader and the profiles do not show a verification gate, a bad output from agent_a can cascade into public posting or account-side mistakes. This is a default-dangerous interaction if chained directly.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a-produced captions, filenames, or scripts without independent verification
IF agent_a's output is used as the source of truth for an upload or posting step
mitigations: Insert a human review checkpoint between agents
Require agent_b to validate filenames and captions against source media
Use a dry-run mode before any real upload
Log and diff agent_a outputs before agent_b acts on them

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles model-provider API keys and runtime files, while agent_b handles account data and uploads to external platforms. The profiles do not specify residency, retention, or DPA terms, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because the data classes differ and the pair can move account/media data into third-party services, medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF account data or media includes regulated personal data
IF either agent stores or uploads data under a policy that differs from the other agent's retention or residency terms
mitigations: Classify the data before running either agent
Keep regulated data out of the upload pipeline
Confirm retention settings for both services
Use separate accounts for sensitive and non-sensitive work
